metadata.title: Various Techniques Used in Connection with Random Digits
metadata.authors: John von Neumann (summary written by George E. Forsythe)
metadata.source_note: Extracted from PDF->text fallback; .tex source not available. Math fidelity reduced.

nodes.name: Problem (A): Random decimal digits
nodes.statement: Produce a sequence of random decimal digits in which each digit appears with probability $1/10$ and consecutive digits are independent in all combinations.

nodes.name: Problem (B): Sampling from an assigned distribution
nodes.statement: Produce random real numbers distributed according to an assigned probability distribution law $f(x)\,dx$ on a given interval (e.g. $(0,1)$).
nodes.statement_clean: Generate i.i.d. samples from a target density $f$.

nodes.name: Sin of arithmetical methods
nodes.statement: Any one who considers arithmetical methods of producing random digits is, of course, in a state of sin: there is no such thing as a random number, only methods to produce them, and a strict arithmetic procedure is not such a method.

nodes.name: Judge cooking recipes by their results
nodes.statement: Arithmetic recipes for producing random digits cannot be justified rigorously and should merely be judged by their results: if the digits work well on one problem, they usually succeed on others of the same type.

nodes.name: Middle-square method (squaring and taking middle digits)
nodes.statement: Form $y = f(x)$ as the middle ten digits of the square of the ten-digit number $x$, and iterate $x_{i+1} = f(x_i)$.
output: Pseudo-random sequence $\{x_i\}$ obtained by repeatedly squaring and extracting middle digits

nodes.name: Ulam's logistic-map iteration
nodes.statement: Iterate the mapping $f(x) = 4x(1-x)$ on $(0,1)$, producing $x_{i+1} = 4 x_i (1 - x_i)$.
nodes.notes: Attributed by von Neumann to Dr. Ulam.

nodes.name: Borel theorem on normal numbers
nodes.statement: For Lebesgue-almost every real $\alpha_1 \in (0,1)$, the binary digits of the iterates $\alpha_{i+1} = 2\alpha_i \bmod 1$ are uniformly distributed on $(0,1)$.
nodes.statement_clean: Almost every real number is normal in binary, so the shift map produces uniformly distributed iterates.
assumptions: $\alpha_1 \in (0,1)$ outside a set of Lebesgue measure zero
nodes.origin_citation: Borel (theorem on randomness of digits of real numbers)

nodes.name: Stationary distribution of the logistic map
nodes.statement: Setting $x_i = \sin^2 \pi \alpha_i$ conjugates the iteration $x_{i+1} = 4 x_i (1-x_i)$ to the doubling map $\alpha_{i+1} = 2 \alpha_i \pmod 1$, so the $x_i$ have density $(2\pi)^{-1} [x(1-x)]^{-1/2}$.
assumptions: $\alpha_1$ outside the Lebesgue-null exceptional set of Borel's theorem
conclusions: The iterates $\{x_i\}$ of $f(x) = 4x(1-x)$ are distributed with density $(2\pi)^{-1}[x(1-x)]^{-1/2}$

nodes.name: Round-off destroys theoretical guarantee
nodes.statement: Since $|f'(x)|$ on $(0,1)$ averages to about 2 for the logistic map, after roughly 33 iterations any round-off error grows past $10^{10}$, so a finite-precision machine is really only testing the random properties of its round-off rule.

nodes.name: Self-perpetuating zeros in the squaring method
nodes.statement: Sequences from the middle-square routine are exposed to the danger of self-perpetuating zeros at the ends of the numbers $x_i$; Forsythe's remark that in some cases the zero mechanism is the major mechanism destroying the sequences is encouraging.

nodes.name: Force the last digit to a 1 to avoid bias
nodes.statement: When converting random binary digits into uniform reals on $(0,1)$, always force the last digit to be a $1$ to avoid the bias from truncation.

nodes.name: Inverse-CDF (inverse transform) sampling
nodes.statement: Given target density $f$ on $(0,1)$ with CDF $F(t) = \int_0^t f(u)\,du$, draw uniform $T \in (0,1)$ and return $X = \Phi(T)$, where $\Phi = F^{-1}$.

nodes.name: Inverse-CDF often cumbersome
nodes.statement: Computing the inverse CDF $\Phi(T)$ for each draw is often cumbersome in practice; other tricks are frequently more efficient when applicable.

nodes.name: Rejection sampling (acceptance-rejection method)
nodes.statement: Choose a scaling factor $a$ with $a f(x) \le 1$; draw uniform pairs $(X, Y)$ on $(0,1)^2$ and accept $X$ when $Y \le a f(X)$, otherwise reject and redraw.
nodes.pseudocode: Repeat: draw $X, Y \sim U(0,1)$; if $Y > a f(X)$ reject and continue; else return $X$.

nodes.name: Efficiency of rejection sampling
nodes.statement: The acceptance ratio is proportional to $f(X)/\max f$; efficiency depends on how close $a f$ comes to its upper bound, the smaller this ratio the more difficult the method.

nodes.name: Implicit acceptance test
nodes.statement: One can often test $Y \le a f(X)$ implicitly without computing $f(X)$: e.g. for $a f(x) = (1 - x^2)^{1/2}$ the test $Y > a f(X)$ becomes simply "is $X^2 + Y^2 > 1$?".

nodes.name: Sampling $\Theta \sim \pi^{-1}(1-\theta^2)^{-1/2}\,d\theta$ on $(-1,1)$
nodes.statement: To sample $\Theta$ with density $\pi^{-1}(1-\theta^2)^{-1/2}$ on $(-1,1)$, the obvious procedure is $\Theta = \sin(\pi T)$ with $T$ uniform on $(-1,1)$, but evaluating a transcendental function of a random number seems silly.

nodes.name: Unit-disk trick for the arcsine distribution
nodes.statement: Draw $X, Y$ uniform on $(0,1)$; reject if $X^2 + Y^2 > 1$; otherwise the angle $\phi = \arctan(X/Y)$ is uniform on $(0, \pi/2)$, and one can return $\sin \phi = \pm X/(X^2+Y^2)^{1/2}$ or, avoiding the square root, $\sin(2\phi - \pi/2) = -\cos 2\phi = (X^2 - Y^2)/(X^2 + Y^2)$.
output: A sample with the arcsine-type distribution; efficiency $\pi/4$
nodes.pseudocode: Repeat: draw $X, Y \sim U(0,1)$; if $X^2 + Y^2 > 1$ reject; else return $(X^2 - Y^2)/(X^2 + Y^2)$ (no square root needed).
nodes.notes: Efficiency stated as $\pi/4$; the square-root form $\pm X/(X^2+Y^2)^{1/2}$ is replaced by the rational form via the double-angle identity.

nodes.name: Sampling from the exponential density $e^{-x}\,dx$
nodes.statement: Generate nonnegative random numbers $X$ with the exponential distribution $e^{-x}\,dx$ on $[0,\infty)$, as needed to represent free paths in slab problems.

nodes.name: Black-Jack / Twenty-one method for the exponential distribution
nodes.statement: Iterative method that generates $X \sim e^{-x}\,dx$ by drawing uniform $Y_i$ until the strictly decreasing chain $Y_1 > Y_2 > \dots > Y_n$ is broken (i.e. $Y_n \le Y_{n+1}$), then accepting $Y_1$ if $n$ is odd and otherwise restarting with an offset incremented by $1$.
nodes.pseudocode: Initialize counter $k \leftarrow 0$. Repeat: draw $Y_1, Y_2, \ldots$ until first index $n$ with $Y_n \le Y_{n+1}$. If $n$ is odd, return $X = k + Y_1$. If $n$ is even, set $k \leftarrow k + 1$ and restart.
nodes.notes: von Neumann compares this to the card game Twenty-one (Black Jack). Each trial uses about $(1+e)(1-e^{-1})^{-1} \approx 6$ values of $Y$, so efficiency is roughly one-sixth.

nodes.name: Probability of a length-$n$ decreasing chain
nodes.statement: Let $E_n$ be the event $Y_1 > Y_2 > \dots > Y_n$ for i.i.d. uniform $Y_i$ on $(0,1)$. Then $\Pr(E_n) = (n!)^{-1}$, and $\Pr\{x < Y_1 < x+dx \mid E_n\} = n x^{n-1}\,dx$.

nodes.name: Proof of length-$n$ chain probability
nodes.statement: By induction on $n$ using the symmetry of i.i.d. uniform variables.

nodes.name: Black-Jack method produces $e^{-x}\,dx$
nodes.statement: The probability of jointly observing $x < Y_1 < x+dx$, the chain event $E_n$, and not $E_{n+1}$ is $[x^{n-1}/(n-1)! - x^n/n!]\,dx$; summing over odd $n$ yields $\Pr\{x < Y_1 < x+dx\} = e^{-x}\,dx$ on $0 \le x \le 1$, and the rejected fraction $e^{-1}$ is handled by repeating with $X$ shifted by an integer.
assumptions: Acceptance rule: keep $Y_1$ when the first violation index $n$ of $Y_1 > Y_2 > \cdots$ is odd
conclusions: The accepted samples $X$ have density $e^{-x}\,dx$ on $[0,\infty)$ when combined with the integer-shift retry rule

nodes.name: Proof that the Black-Jack method generates $e^{-x}\,dx$
nodes.statement: Combine Lemma LP386.1 with summation over odd $n$ and the retry rule that increments $X$ by $1$ on rejection.

nodes.name: Joint probability of $E_n$ and not $E_{n+1}$
nodes.statement: By Lemma LP386.1, $\Pr\{x < Y_1 < x+dx,\ E_n,\ \text{not } E_{n+1}\} = [x^{n-1}/(n-1)! - x^n/n!]\,dx$.

nodes.name: Sum over odd $n$
nodes.statement: Summing the joint probability over odd $n$ gives $\Pr\{x < Y_1 < x+dx\} = e^{-x}\,dx$ on $0 \le x \le 1$.

nodes.name: Extension by integer shifts
nodes.statement: The rejected fraction $e^{-1}$ is handled by reusing the next $Y_1$ on retry, taking $X = Y_1 + 1$ if accepted on the first retry, $X = Y_1 + 2$ on the second, etc., since $e^{-x}\,dx = e^{-1} e^{-x+1}\,dx$, which extends the density to all $x \ge 0$.

nodes.name: Expected number of trials and overall efficiency
nodes.statement: A calculation shows that one may expect about $(1+e)(1-e^{-1})^{-1} \approx 6$ values of $Y$ for each $X$ accepted; the efficiency is thus about one-sixth, and the machine has effectively computed a logarithm using only comparisons.

nodes.name: ENIAC was faster with truncated $\log(1-T)$
nodes.statement: Under ENIAC's particular conditions it was slightly quicker to use a truncated power series for $\log(1-T)$ than to perform all the discriminations of the Black-Jack method.

nodes.name: Generalization to first-order ODEs
nodes.statement: The above method can be modified to yield a distribution satisfying any first-order differential equation.
